description:
Kỷ nguyên Vin Mừng is joining NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 with “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.” We aim to create an online game that introduces young learners to space exploration and astronaut training through fun, interactive missions.

Leader: Pham Phu Hung – phuhung0707dzz@gmail.com

Members: Nguyen Truong Giang – truonggiang2624@gmail.com; Bui Quynh Anh – gevbui1509@gmail.com; Le Gia Bach – legiabach39@gmail.com; Nguyen Tung Lam – nl13032004@gmail.com.
summary:
Lunar Frontier is an educational adventure game where players experience the challenges of building and managing a research base on the Moon. Designed for players aged 7 and above, the game makes space science more approachable through storytelling, exploration, and meaningful choices.

In the game, players become the Commander of LUNA-1, a small lunar research station. Over seven mission days, they work alongside two astronauts and an AI assistant to keep the base running while facing unexpected challenges, such as lunar dust covering solar panels, oxygen system problems, and dangerous solar radiation.

But there's a catch: you can't do everything at once.

Every decision comes with a trade-off. Should you save energy for emergencies or use it to grow food? Should you focus on scientific discoveries or make sure your crew has enough resources to survive? Your choices affect the base, your research progress, and how the story ends.

As players complete missions, they gradually unlock different parts of the lunar base and discover how science and engineering work together in space exploration.

Using scientific information and educational resources from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency, we want to turn real space challenges into something young people can explore and learn from.

Our goal is simple: We don't just want players to learn facts about the Moon. We want them to experience what it's like to make difficult decisions, solve problems, and think like real astronauts.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? Lunar Horizon is an interactive, scenario-based educational web game designed for learners aged 12 and above, focusing on life support, resource management, and survival decision-making on a lunar research outpost (LUNA-1). Players act as the Commander navigating through the first 7 Sols, facing critical emergency dilemmas such as solar panel lunar dust accumulation, life support hull breaches, and high-energy solar radiation storms.

What benefits and intended impact does it have? The project aims to spark youth interest in STEM, space exploration, and aerospace science by bridging complex NASA/CSA space datasets with gamified problem-solving. Players learn practical survival science and develop critical thinking by balancing mission research objectives with crew safety and resource conservation (cause-and-effect mechanics).

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend & Architecture: Web technologies (HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript/React) structured for smooth interactive UI/UX and responsive deployment.
  • Data Sources & APIs: Integrated open data resources from NASA and international space agencies, including NASA CCMC DONKI (Space Weather & Solar Particle Event alerts), NASA OSDR RadLab (Radiation dosimetry and shielding data), NASA OSDR Biological Repository (Plant growth and life support stress responses), and the CSA Food Production Toolkit (Lunar greenhouse environmental constraints).

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider? Lunar Horizon moves away from dry, text-based quizzes by employing an immersive "Choice-Consequence-Science Note" framework. We carefully balanced scientific accuracy with age-appropriate gameplay, ensuring that abstract concepts—like electrostatic regolith adhesion, oxygen electrolysis maintenance, and solar radiation shielding—are intuitively understood through high-stakes command decisions.
